tldr: The authors developed FasTac, a compact curved vision-based tactile sensor combining RGB and near-infrared (NIR) light, achieving high-precision 3D shape reconstruction, three-axis contact force estimation, and an ultra-fast, low-latency feedback of 1.09 ms via an FPGA.
hero_caption: Grasping a strawberry with a multi-fingered hand equipped with FasTac. From multispectral RGB and NIR images captured by a single CMOS image sensor, the sensor finely captures the strawberry's surface details (normals and depth) alongside the contact force distribution on the curved surface.
overview:
For dexterous robotic manipulation, rounded fingertips like human fingers must perceive fine surface details, separate normal loads from shear loads to avoid slipping, and capture transient contact phenomena such as vibrations without delay.

However, conventional vision-based tactile sensors combining a camera and an elastomer have largely focused on flat geometries. When fingertips are made curved, internal illumination fails to reach uniformly, causing shadows that break 3D shape reconstruction. In addition, elastomer stiffness and deformation characteristics vary across different positions on the curved surface, making accurate contact force estimation extremely challenging. Furthermore, streaming high-resolution images to an external PC or GPU introduces communication and buffering latencies that cannot keep up with fast contact control.

To overcome these three hurdles simultaneously, the authors propose FasTac, a curved vision-based tactile sensor. On the hardware side, it combines a single RGB-IR image sensor with four illumination colors (RGB plus near-infrared light) to achieve parallax-free multispectral imaging. This prevents shadow-induced information loss even on curved surfaces, and by solving a fast Poisson equation integrated with boundary priors, it reconstructs high-precision 3D depth.

For contact force estimation, the authors designed HyperForce, a dynamic convolution model inspired by the finite element method (FEM). It models local stiffness variations based on contact locations and accurately decouples and estimates three-axis forces. Furthermore, this pipeline was deployed onto an FPGA directly connected to the sensor, executing the entire process from image capture to normal force $F_z$ estimation in just 1.09 ms.

Experiments show that depth reconstruction error dropped to 0.0415 mm, with both shear and normal forces estimated at around 2% error. The authors also demonstrated adaptive grasping that instantly increases grip force upon slip detection, as well as the measurement of high-frequency vibrations up to 100 Hz.
contributions: Combined a single RGB-IR image sensor with RGB+NIR illumination to achieve parallax-free, compact 3D normal and depth reconstruction without shadow degradation, even on high-curvature surfaces.

Proposed HyperForce, a coordinate-adaptive dynamic convolution network that models position-dependent stiffness changes across the curved elastomer, achieving high-precision three-axis force estimation.
Fully deployed the complete pipeline from image acquisition to 3D reconstruction and normal force $F_z$ estimation onto an FPGA, demonstrating an ultra-low latency of 1.09 ms.

sections.heading: Toward Dexterous Fingertips: The Challenge of Combining Curvature, 3-Axis Force, and Ultra-Low Latency
sections.summary: Dexterous robot manipulation demands fine 3D shape perception on curved fingertips, decoupling of normal and shear forces, and latency-free high-speed processing. This paper presents the concept of FasTac, a novel curved vision-based tactile sensor that tackles all three challenges simultaneously.
sections.details:
In dexterous manipulation, fingertip contact occurs not on flat planes but across small, curved regions, with contact conditions shifting from moment to moment. Capturing minute textures and edges requires high spatial resolution, while holding objects without dropping them requires accurately grasping not only normal forces but also tangential frictional forces (shear forces). Furthermore, responding promptly to transient events such as collisions and vibrations requires squeezing sensing-to-feedback latency to the absolute minimum.

However, existing tactile sensors fail to deliver all of these together. Array sensors, such as piezoresistive or capacitive types, suffer from complex wiring and low spatial resolution, making detailed 3D shape reconstruction impossible. On the other hand, vision-based tactile sensors using cameras (such as GelSight) offer high resolution, but have mostly been flat. When fingertips are curved, light path issues cause local shadows (self-occlusion) that frequently break 3D reconstruction. Moreover, because the rubber's curvature and thickness differ across locations, the mechanical models that back-calculate forces from deformation become intricately coupled.

Additionally, the traditional workflow of sending high-resolution images to a PC or GPU for processing suffers from communication and driver-scheduling jitter, preventing integration into high-speed control loops. Against this backdrop, FasTac was created by fusing a multispectral optical system, a position-adaptive force estimation AI, and edge FPGA acceleration within a compact curved fingertip.

sections.heading: Hurdles in Prior Work: Insufficient Light, Curved Non-Uniformity, and the Lack of Edge Processing
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work across three domains of vision-based tactile sensing: 3D shape reconstruction, contact force estimation, and computational acceleration. It highlights the optical and mechanical challenges of curved geometries and the computational limits of relying on external PCs.
sections.details:
Related work broadly divides into three streams:

- **Vision-based tactile 3D reconstruction**: Photometric stereo, which recovers surface normals from multi-directional lighting shading, is widely used. However, on curved surfaces, light intensity becomes non-uniform and information is lost. GelSight360, which placed cross-LEDs inside to illuminate the entire circumference, partially blocked the field of view. GelSplitter3D, which split near-infrared light using a beam splitter, required multiple cameras, suffering from larger form factors and misalignment issues.
- **Contact force estimation**: Approaches to estimating forces from elastomer deformation include physics-based and deep-learning-based methods. While stiffness matrix identification via FEM and CNN regression from image features have been proposed, no prior method explicitly accounts for the spatial non-uniformity of curved elastomers—where stiffness and boundary constraints vary depending on contact location.
- **Tactile processing acceleration**: Efforts such as using event cameras (EveTac) or lightweight CNNs (MinSight) have been explored, but they remain bound by the transfer and scheduling latencies of host PC CPUs and GPUs. Although attempts have been made to connect in-finger cameras directly to FPGAs to reduce communication overhead, none have completed the entire pipeline from image acquisition to 3D reconstruction and contact force estimation entirely on the edge.

FasTac provides a comprehensive answer to these unresolved issues through single-sensor RGB-NIR imaging, a location-aware dynamic CNN, and end-to-end FPGA processing.

sections.heading: Hardware Engineering: A Compact Fingertip Capturing RGB and Infrared Simultaneously with One Camera
sections.summary: This section describes the mechanical design that integrates optics, illumination, and an elastomer within the limited space of a fingertip. Using a single RGB-IR sensor, four-color LEDs, and the scattering properties of the skeleton, a uniform, compact curved fingertip is realized.
sections.details:
FasTac's mechanical design prioritized compactness and high integration so that it could be embedded as a robot hand fingertip. The sensor body consists primarily of three components: a light-guiding skeleton housing the camera, a flexible printed circuit (FPC) carrying multispectral LEDs, and an elastomer skin (gel).

- **Imaging module**: An ultra-compact RGB-IR CMOS sensor, the OmniVision OV2736, is employed. A specialized 4×4 color filter array (CFA) is arranged across the pixels, allowing simultaneous capture of visible light (RGB) and near-infrared light (NIR) in a single exposure. Because it does not use optical splitters like prisms, it provides parallax-free images with perfectly aligned optical axes, directly contributing to sensor miniaturization.
- **Illumination system**: In addition to standard RGB light sources, an NIR LED was introduced as an independent fourth channel. As a result, even if certain light paths are restricted on a curved surface, more than three independent illumination directions required for photometric stereo are stably secured. RGB and NIR LEDs are arranged orthogonally across the four corners of an FPC contoured to the fingertip's curve. Illuminating from behind the translucent photosensitive resin skeleton gently diffuses the point-source light, drastically suppressing specular highlights.
- **Tactile skin**: A soft gel that deforms sensitively even under tiny contacts was fabricated by blending platinum-cure silicone (Solaris) with a softener (Slacker) at a high-concentration ratio of 1:1:3. To prevent 3D-printing layer lines from transferring to the surface, precision acrylic (PMMA) was used for the mold. Furthermore, silver powder was uniformly sprayed on the surface to form a high-reflectivity, ambient-light-blocking layer, and a black marker dot array was engraved via laser micromachining to capture tangential displacements.

(a) Exploded view showing the cover, curved FPC with LEDs including NIR, translucent skeleton, smooth gel molded from acrylic, and the ultra-compact camera at the bottom. (b) Cross-sectional view showing how rear LED light diffuses through the skeleton to uniformly illuminate the surface.

sections.heading: Algorithm: Multispectral 3D Reconstruction and Position-Aware Dynamic Convolution via HyperForce
sections.summary: This section explains the algorithms for reconstructing 3D shape and three-axis contact forces from images, as well as their FPGA implementation. The core elements are normal estimation via an MLP incorporating positional coordinates, CAD boundary-constrained Poisson integration, and FEM-inspired dynamic kernel force estimation.
sections.details:
The pipeline that derives 3D shape and contact forces from images is grounded in an elegant integration of geometry and mechanics.

### Multispectral 3D Shape Reconstruction
RAW10 images from the sensor undergo preprocessing, such as crosstalk removal, and are separated into individual RGB and NIR channels. Because the distance and angle to light sources differ across pixels on a curved surface, simple photometric calculations can confuse shadows with surface tilt. Therefore, four-color intensities along with normalized pixel coordinates $(u, v)$ are fed into a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to estimate pixel-wise, high-precision surface normal vectors $\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}$.
Integrating normals into depth uses the Poisson equation. However, the standard fast solver assumption—that boundary depth is zero—does not hold on a curved fingertip. To address this, boundary geometry derived from the sensor's CAD model is incorporated as prior information (Dirichlet boundary condition) into the right-hand side of the equation. Solving this rapidly via discrete sine transform (DST-I) yields accurate, drift-free 3D shapes.

### FEM-Inspired Dynamic Convolution: HyperForce
Contact force estimation builds a 3D displacement field $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{p})$ by fusing tangential displacement (shear) from marker tracking with normal displacement obtained from reconstructed depth. Because curved gel thickness and constraints vary spatially, identical displacements yield different contact forces depending on contact location.
Inspired by FEM, where nodal forces are computed by multiplying a stiffness matrix with a displacement vector, the authors structured convolution operations over local displacement patches. However, because local stiffness patterns are not translation-invariant, a hypernetwork was designed to dynamically generate convolution kernels from the contact location's 3D coordinates rather than using a static CNN. This is HyperForce. Utilizing position-dependent optimal kernels naturally captures the curved surface's non-uniform mechanical response, outputting accurate three-axis forces ($F_x, F_y, F_z$).

### Edge Implementation on FPGA
The estimation pipeline for normal force $F_z$, which is most crucial for high-rate contact control, was fully implemented as streaming hardware on the programmable logic (PL) of a Xilinx MPSoC (FPGA). The MLP runs on pipelined matrix-vector compute units, while Poisson integration efficiently executes 1D DSTs along rows and columns using ping-pong buffers. Storing kernels in on-chip ROM enables an architecture that accumulates forces almost synchronously as pixels stream in, without buffering full frames into external memory.

captions.F4: Overall pipeline for 3D shape reconstruction and three-axis contact force estimation from images. Shows (a) multispectral normal estimation and boundary-constrained Poisson integration (top-left), (b) shear displacement extraction via marker tracking (bottom-left), and (c) three-axis force accumulation via coordinate-adaptive dynamic convolution (HyperForce, right).

sections.heading: Hardware Experiments: 0.04 mm Fine Geometry Perception, Anti-Slip Grasping, and 100 Hz Vibration Detection
sections.summary: Using an automated contact data collection platform, the authors demonstrated the performance of geometric reconstruction, three-axis force estimation, anti-slip adaptive grasp control, and FPGA-driven ultra-fast vibration measurement.
sections.details:
An automated calibration setup combining a CNC stage and an ATI high-precision 6-axis force sensor was built to collect strictly non-overlapping training and testing datasets with a spherical indenter.

- **3D geometric reconstruction performance**: In tests with a 5 mm diameter (2.5 mm radius) spherical indenter, adding NIR light reduced gradient mean absolute error (MAE) by approximately 30%. Furthermore, applying CAD boundary priors dramatically improved depth reconstruction MAE from 0.2730 mm (RGB-only, no prior) down to **0.0415 mm**, slashing the error by roughly a factor of six. Surface seeds on a strawberry, fingerprint ridges, and fine patterns on an LED board were all clearly reconstructed.
- **Three-axis contact force estimation accuracy**: Compared against ground truth from the ATI sensor, normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) for $F_x, F_y, F_z$ reached 2.37%, 2.41%, and 2.74%, respectively (coefficient of determination $R^2$ between 0.969 and 0.992), showing high linearity and precision. Ablation experiments confirmed that HyperForce's dynamic kernels (MAE: 0.0545 N) substantially outperformed a standard static CNN ($F_z$ MAE: 0.4905 N), and that feeding both tangential and normal displacements is essential.
- **Adaptive grasping with friction coefficient feedback**: Experiments were conducted grasping a plastic bottle with a robot hand while applying downward disturbance impulses. FasTac monitored the real-time friction coefficient $\mu = F_s / F_n$ from normal force $F_n$ and shear force $F_s$, triggering finger joints to tighten the instant a threshold was exceeded. Without feedback, the disturbance caused the bottle to slip out; with feedback, detecting slip precursors allowed instant grasp force increases, keeping the object securely held.
- **Edge deployment and vibration response**: On the FPGA, processing latency from image input to $F_z$ output reached just **1.09 ms** (fully keeping pace with the ~240 Hz frame rate at an energy consumption of 8.41 mJ/frame). This substantially outperforms GPU latency of 3.26 ms (33.60 mJ) and CPU latency of 6.82 ms (238.05 mJ). In dynamic experiments with a mechanical shaker, the CPU suffered aliasing at 70 Hz, and the GPU failed to follow at 100 Hz. In contrast, the FPGA accurately preserved the 100 Hz frequency peak and temporal periodicity.

captions.F7: Comparison of 3D reconstruction results on real objects (strawberry, fingerprint, micro LED array). Compared to RGB-only illumination, RGB+NIR multispectral illumination (far right) reconstructs surface dimples, fine ridges, and step edges clearly and continuously.
captions.F9: Time-series curves of contact forces, friction coefficient, and motor angle during adaptive bottle grasping. (a) Without feedback, external disturbances cause slippage (forces and friction coefficient drop sharply at point a3). (b) With friction coefficient feedback, motor angles close whenever disturbances occur, instantly preventing slip.

sections.heading: Summary: A New Generation of Fast, High-Precision Tactile Fingertips in the Palm of Your Hand
sections.summary: FasTac sets a new benchmark for curved tactile fingertips by integrating RGB-NIR optics, boundary-conditioned 3D reconstruction, position-adaptive force estimation, and FPGA acceleration.
sections.details:
This paper presented FasTac, a vision-based tactile sensor integrating high-precision 3D geometry perception, reliable three-axis force estimation, and ultra-low-latency real-time processing within a compact curved fingertip for dexterous robotic manipulation.

Simultaneous RGB-NIR capture with a single CMOS sensor and CAD boundary priors enabled minute texture reconstruction with a depth error of 0.0415 mm. In addition, HyperForce, which addresses curved gel stiffness non-uniformity via dynamic convolution, decoupled normal and shear forces with errors around 2%. Furthermore, end-to-end FPGA deployment of the pipeline realized normal force feedback with an ultra-short latency of 1.09 ms.

Demonstrating everything from fine texture perception to reflexive anti-slip grasp control and high-frequency vibration detection, this work marks a significant milestone toward practical multi-fingered robotic hands.

sections.heading: Appendix: Auto-Calibration Environment Details and High-Frequency Shaker Benchmarks on FPGA
sections.summary: This section covers the CNC-based data collection protocol, the experimental setup for high-frequency vibration testing with a shaker, and detailed performance comparison data across CPU, GPU, and FPGA.
sections.details:
The paper's supplementary material provides key details regarding experimental reproducibility and edge deployment:

- **Automated data collection protocol**: Four reference corner points were defined on the CNC stage, and grid points were generated within the active sensing area via bilinear interpolation. At each point, normal preloads of 0.5 N, 1.0 N, and 1.5 N were applied, along with four directions of in-plane shear forces ($F_h = 0.3F_z$ and $0.6F_z$). The training, validation, and testing datasets used completely spatially separated grids of 8×8, 5×5, and 8×8, strictly eliminating data leakage and overfitting.
- **FPGA edge implementation conditions**: While offline experiments used full-resolution images (1920×1080), the real-time FPGA deployment cropped and downsampled a region of interest (ROI) to 128×128 pixels to meet memory constraints and boost frame rates. This optimization reduced the camera readout window, enabling high-speed 240 Hz sampling.
- **Frequency analysis of vibration shaker tests**: Dynamic contacts were evaluated using a shaker platform oscillating vertically with sinusoidal motion. Against the sensor sampling frequency $f_s = 240$ Hz, the CPU output $F_z$ at 104 Hz (Nyquist limit 52 Hz), the GPU at 156 Hz (limit 78 Hz), and the FPGA at 240 Hz (limit 120 Hz). Peak detection via Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) revealed that at an excitation frequency of 70 Hz, the CPU suffered aliasing to 31.58 Hz, and at 100 Hz, the GPU misidentified it as 49.39 Hz. Only the FPGA consistently detected 100.04 Hz accurately.

captions.F10: Platform for high-frequency vibration testing. (a) Frequency controller and top view, (b) side view of the shaker probe periodically loading the FasTac surface vertically. This setup was used to evaluate dynamic contact responses up to 100 Hz.

takeaways: In curved vision-based tactile sensors, introducing NIR light via an RGB-IR sensor is a highly practical solution to compensate for local shadowing.

Because stiffness variations across contact locations cannot be ignored in curved elastomers, dynamic convolution that generates kernels on the fly from coordinate encodings is exceptionally effective for force estimation.
The tactile sensing pipeline (normal estimation to Poisson integration to force estimation) maps naturally to FPGA streaming architectures, achieving deterministic ultra-low latencies around 1 ms.
limitations: Full-pipeline FPGA deployment is currently limited to normal force $F_z$; complete FPGA implementation of three-axis forces ($F_x, F_y$) remains future work due to the complexity of marker tracking.
Because images are downsampled to 128×128 for FPGA processing, there is a trade-off in fine texture reconstruction accuracy compared to full-resolution offline processing.
Long-term evaluations regarding gel durability, wear, and drifts in silicone viscoelastic properties due to temperature changes are not discussed.
